_comment: Key policy for the biometric CMK -- the key that, in the master plan's
words, keeps the embeddings 'mathematically indecipherable without the
distinct encryption keys held securely within the AWS Key Management
Service'.
aws kms create-key --policy file://deploy/iam/kms-key-policy.json \
--description 'PNSM biometric embedding CMK' \
--key-usage ENCRYPT_DECRYPT --key-spec SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT
A KMS key policy is not like other resource policies: it is the ROOT of
authority for the key. If the account root is not granted here, IAM
policies elsewhere in the account grant nothing at all, and the key
becomes unmanageable. That is what the first statement is for -- it is not
boilerplate, and removing it is unrecoverable.
Separation of duties. The administrator can rotate, tag, schedule
deletion and audit the key; the administrator cannot Decrypt with it.
For a key protecting biometric data that split is the point: managing
the key and reading employees' faces are different jobs, and nobody
should hold both by default.
The only principal that ever handles a plaintext embedding key. The
encryption-context condition is enforced here as well as in the task
role: a key policy condition holds even if somebody later attaches a
broader identity policy, so this is the copy that actually guarantees
the property.
Selfies, not embeddings -- a different data path with a different
encryption context (S3 supplies its own), which is why it needs its own
statement. Scoped by via-service so this grant is unusable except
through S3.
Scheduling this key for deletion destroys every enrolment in the
system -- there is no backup of a KMS key material, by design. The
recovery from that mistake is re-enrolling every employee, so it is
worth a hardware second factor. Seven to thirty days of pending
deletion is the only safety net after this point.
